title: Tiredness and breathlessness in a 58-year-old man
opening_brief:
You are a medical student in the medicine outpatient department.

A 58-year-old man has been referred by a general practitioner with a haemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL found on a routine test. He has come in for an opinion.

Anaemia is a finding, not a diagnosis. Your job is to work out why.

patient.name: Mohan Das
patient.background: Married, two grown children. Fairly sedentary.

persona.speech_style: Polite, measured, slightly formal. Answers exactly what is asked.
persona.emotional_state: Not particularly worried; thinks the test was a mistake because he feels 'basically fine'.
knows_not: whether he has ever had a colonoscopy
the name of the painkiller he takes for his knee beyond 'a red tablet'
quirks: Minimises symptoms — says he is 'fine' until asked about specific activities.
Mentions the change in bowel habit only if asked directly; he considers it too minor and too embarrassing to bring up.

chief_complaint: referred with a low haemoglobin found on a routine blood test

present_illness.onset: He cannot date it. Looking back, he has been slowing down for perhaps six months.
present_illness.character: General tiredness. Breathless walking up the two flights of stairs at work, which never used to trouble him.
present_illness.severity: Enough that he now takes the lift, but he did not think it was worth mentioning.
associated: bowels have changed over about four months — looser, going three or four times a day when he used to go once
sometimes feels he has not fully emptied his bowels
lost about 5 kg over six months without trying
an odd craving to chew ice
present_illness.progression: Very gradual and steady. Nothing sudden.

past_medical: Osteoarthritis of the right knee for four years
Borderline high blood pressure, not on treatment
Piles diagnosed about ten years ago, occasional bleeding then, nothing recently that he has noticed
No known ulcer, no previous surgery
medications: A red painkiller tablet for the knee, almost daily for the past two years — he thinks it is diclofenac
family: Father died at 66 of 'a growth in the stomach or intestine' — he was never told exactly which
No family history of coeliac disease
social: Non-vegetarian, eats a mixed diet, no dietary restriction
Drinks alcohol perhaps twice a month
Smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 20 years, stopped 8 years ago
No travel abroad, no exposure to lead or industrial chemicals
review_of_systems_positive: occasional mild cramping in the left lower abdomen
feels cold more easily than he used to
review_of_systems_negative: no black tarry stools that he has noticed
no fresh bleeding per rectum recently
no joint pains other than the knee
no numbness or tingling in the hands or feet

examination.label: Vital signs
examination.result: Pulse 96/min regular. BP 128/80 mmHg, no postural drop. Respiratory rate 18/min. SpO2 98% on room air. Temperature 36.8 C.

examination.label: General examination for signs of anaemia
examination.result: Marked conjunctival and palmar pallor. Koilonychia of several fingernails. Angular stomatitis at both corners of the mouth. Atrophic glossitis. No icterus, no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy, no purpura.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.result: Hyperdynamic apex. A soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, grade 2/6 — a flow murmur. Heart sounds otherwise normal. JVP not raised. No pedal oedema.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.result: Soft. A vague, mildly tender fullness in the left iliac fossa; no discrete mass definitely palpable. Liver and spleen not enlarged. No ascites.

examination.label: Per-rectal examination
examination.result: External haemorrhoids present, not bleeding. No rectal mass palpable within reach. Stool on the glove is dark brown; faecal occult blood on that sample is positive.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.result: Clear, equal air entry, no added sounds.

examination.label: Neurological examination
examination.result: Normal tone, power and reflexes. Vibration and joint position sense intact — no evidence of subacute combined degeneration.

investigations.label: Complete blood count with indices and peripheral smear
investigations.result: Hb 7.6 g/dL. MCV 66 fL. MCH 20 pg. MCHC 28 g/dL. RDW 19.8%. WBC 6,900/uL, normal differential. Platelets 486,000/uL. Smear: microcytic hypochromic red cells with anisopoikilocytosis and pencil cells. Reticulocyte count 1.2% (inadequate for the degree of anaemia).

investigations.label: Iron studies
investigations.result: Serum ferritin 6 ng/mL. Serum iron 22 mcg/dL. TIBC 468 mcg/dL. Transferrin saturation 4.7%. Diagnostic of iron deficiency.

investigations.label: Vitamin B12 and folate
investigations.result: B12 402 pg/mL, folate 8.1 ng/mL — both normal, so this is a pure iron deficiency rather than a dimorphic anaemia.

investigations.label: Colonoscopy with biopsy
investigations.result: An ulcerated, partly circumferential mass at 28 cm from the anal verge in the sigmoid colon, narrowing the lumen but traversable. Biopsies taken. Remainder of the colon normal; no other polyps.

investigations.label: Histopathology of the biopsy
investigations.result: Moderately differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma. Mismatch repair proteins retained on immunohistochemistry.

investigations.label: Upper GI endoscopy
investigations.result: Mild antral gastritis with two small erosions, consistent with chronic NSAID use. No ulcer, no varices, no mass. Duodenal biopsies taken.

investigations.label: Duodenal biopsy for coeliac disease
investigations.result: Anti-tTG IgA negative with normal total IgA. Duodenal histology normal — coeliac disease excluded.

investigations.label: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
investigations.result: Circumferential sigmoid wall thickening over 5 cm with pericolic fat stranding and two enlarged regional nodes. No liver or lung metastases. Staged as T3 N1 M0.

investigations.label: Carcinoembryonic antigen
investigations.result: CEA 8.4 ng/mL (raised). Useful as a baseline for follow-up, not for diagnosis.

investigations.label: Liver and renal function
investigations.result: Albumin 3.4 g/dL. Bilirubin, transaminases, urea and creatinine all normal.

investigations.label: Haemoglobin electrophoresis (HPLC)
investigations.result: Deferred until after iron repletion. HbA2 1.9% on the sample taken while iron deficient — uninterpretable in this state, and to be repeated after treatment.
investigations.note: Iron deficiency suppresses HbA2 and can mask beta-thalassaemia trait. Order it after iron replacement, not before.

investigations.label: Cross-match and packed cell transfusion
investigations.result: Two units cross-matched. He is haemodynamically stable and not actively bleeding.
investigations.note: Chronic iron deficiency anaemia in a stable patient is corrected with oral or intravenous iron, not with transfusion. Transfusing first also removes the chance to interpret the indices.

differentials.why: Hb 7.6 with MCV 66, a high RDW, pencil cells, ferritin 6 and transferrin saturation 4.7%, with koilonychia, angular stomatitis and pica for ice.

The cause of the iron deficiency, and the diagnosis this case is really about. Iron deficiency anaemia in a man over 50 is gastrointestinal blood loss from a malignancy until proved otherwise — supported here by four months of altered bowel habit, tenesmus, 5 kg weight loss, a positive occult blood test and a family history.

Two years of near-daily diclofenac is a genuine and sufficient explanation for iron deficiency — which is exactly why it is dangerous. Accepting it without a colonoscopy is how a curable cancer gets missed.

He has known piles, and they are visible on examination. Haemorrhoids rarely cause iron deficiency of this severity, and attributing rectal bleeding to piles without visualising the colon is a classic and serious error.
A recognised cause of iron deficiency at any age and worth excluding with serology and duodenal biopsy, both negative here.

The other common cause of a very low MCV in India. Distinguished by a normal or high ferritin, a disproportionately low MCV for the haemoglobin, a normal RDW and a raised HbA2. Here the ferritin of 6 settles it.
Can be microcytic, but ferritin is normal or raised and TIBC is low — the opposite of the pattern here.

Not an acceptable explanation in a non-vegetarian adult man with an adequate diet. Dietary iron deficiency is a diagnosis of exclusion in men and post-menopausal women, and never before the gut has been examined.

final_diagnosis: Severe iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 7.6 g/dL, ferritin 6 ng/mL) due to chronic occult blood loss from a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon, staged T3 N1 M0 — with chronic NSAID use as a contributing but insufficient explanation
diagnosis_reasoning: The blood picture is unambiguous: microcytic, hypochromic, high RDW, pencil cells, ferritin 6 and transferrin saturation under 5%. Ferritin below 15 ng/mL is diagnostic of iron deficiency and excludes thalassaemia trait and anaemia of chronic disease as the primary problem. The important reasoning step is what follows: in a 58-year-old man with no menstrual or dietary explanation, iron deficiency means gastrointestinal blood loss and mandates visualisation of both the upper and lower gut. Two years of diclofenac is a plausible decoy, and the antral erosions found on gastroscopy would have satisfied a less careful clinician. The history that overrides it is four months of altered bowel habit with tenesmus, 5 kg of unintentional weight loss, a left iliac fossa fullness, a positive faecal occult blood test and a father who died of a gastrointestinal malignancy. Colonoscopy shows the sigmoid tumour and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma.

history.label: Change in bowel habit
history.teaching_note: A four-month change in bowel habit in a man over 50 is a red-flag symptom in its own right. He will not volunteer it.

history.label: Bleeding per rectum, melaena and haematemesis
history.teaching_note: Both ends of the gut must be asked about. Note that occult bleeding by definition produces no visible change — a negative answer does not exclude it.

history.label: Unintentional weight loss and appetite
history.teaching_note: Five kilograms over six months without trying is a cancer red flag and shifts the entire probability.

history.label: NSAID, aspirin and anticoagulant use
history.teaching_note: Two years of daily diclofenac is real and relevant — but it is a contributory factor, not a licence to skip the colonoscopy.

history.label: Dietary history and iron intake
history.teaching_note: Establishes whether a dietary explanation is even plausible. In this patient it is not.

history.label: Family history of gastrointestinal cancer
history.teaching_note: A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer roughly doubles the risk and lowers the threshold for colonoscopy.

history.label: Exertional symptoms and functional capacity
history.teaching_note: Quantifying exercise tolerance is how you judge whether chronic anaemia is being tolerated or is decompensating.

history.label: Pica and unusual cravings
history.teaching_note: Pica, especially pagophagia, is specific for iron deficiency and disappears within days of iron replacement.

history.label: Tenesmus and incomplete evacuation
history.teaching_note: Tenesmus localises the pathology to the rectum or distal colon.

history.label: Neurological symptoms of B12 deficiency
history.teaching_note: Separates a pure iron deficiency from a dimorphic or B12-deficient anaemia.

history.label: Previous anaemia, endoscopy or surgery
history.teaching_note: Prior investigations shape how much further work is needed and whether this is recurrent.

history.label: Urinary and other sources of blood loss
history.teaching_note: Iron is lost from wherever blood is lost; the gut is the commonest site but not the only one.

examination.label: Signs of iron deficiency: pallor, koilonychia, glossitis, angular stomatitis
examination.teaching_note: These four signs together make the diagnosis of chronic iron deficiency at the bedside, before any blood test comes back.

examination.label: Per-rectal examination
examination.teaching_note: Mandatory in anyone with iron deficiency or altered bowel habit. Omitting it is the commonest examination failure in this presentation, and here it yields both a positive occult blood result and reassurance that the tumour is out of finger reach.

examination.label: Abdominal examination for a mass and organomegaly
examination.teaching_note: A left iliac fossa mass and hepatomegaly would each change the diagnosis and the staging immediately.

examination.label: Vital signs including postural blood pressure
examination.teaching_note: Distinguishes chronic compensated anaemia from acute blood loss requiring resuscitation.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.teaching_note: A hyperdynamic circulation with a flow murmur is expected; signs of failure would change the transfusion threshold.

examination.label: Lymph node examination
examination.teaching_note: A left supraclavicular node would suggest advanced intra-abdominal malignancy.

examination.label: Neurological examination for posterior column signs
examination.teaching_note: Excludes concurrent B12 deficiency, which would change treatment.

investigations.label: Complete blood count with indices and smear
investigations.teaching_note: The MCV, RDW and smear direct the entire subsequent workup. Never accept a bare haemoglobin value.

investigations.label: Iron studies including ferritin
investigations.teaching_note: Ferritin below 15 ng/mL is diagnostic of iron deficiency. Remember ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be falsely normal with inflammation.

investigations.label: Colonoscopy
investigations.teaching_note: The single investigation that makes the diagnosis. In a man over 50 with iron deficiency, it is mandatory whatever the gastroscopy shows.

investigations.label: Upper GI endoscopy
investigations.teaching_note: Both ends of the gut must be examined. Finding gastritis at the top does not excuse skipping the bottom — and up to 10% of patients have a lesion at each end.

investigations.label: Faecal occult blood test
investigations.teaching_note: A positive result supports gastrointestinal loss; a negative result never excludes it, because bleeding from a tumour is intermittent.

investigations.label: Vitamin B12 and folate
investigations.teaching_note: Confirms a pure rather than a dimorphic anaemia, and a dimorphic picture can mask microcytosis by normalising the MCV.

investigations.label: Coeliac serology
investigations.teaching_note: Recommended in all adults with unexplained iron deficiency, and easily added to the gastroscopy as duodenal biopsies.

investigations.label: Biopsy and histopathology
investigations.teaching_note: No cancer is diagnosed on appearance alone; tissue is required before any treatment decision.

investigations.label: Staging CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
investigations.teaching_note: Staging determines whether surgery is curative and whether neoadjuvant therapy is needed.

investigations.label: Liver function tests
investigations.teaching_note: A screen for hepatic metastases and a marker of nutritional state.

hints: Look at the red cell indices, not just the haemoglobin. What kind of anaemia is this, and what does that narrow it to?
You have established iron deficiency in a 58-year-old man who eats meat and does not menstruate. Where must the iron be going, and what does that oblige you to do?
Review the mandatory investigation of iron deficiency anaemia in men and post-menopausal women, and why a plausible explanation at one end of the gut does not excuse you from examining the other.
teaching_points: Anaemia is a finding, never a final diagnosis. The question is always why.
Classify first by MCV, then by iron studies. Ferritin below 15 ng/mL is diagnostic of iron deficiency; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may be falsely normal in inflammation.
Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or a post-menopausal woman means gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and requires both upper and lower endoscopy.
Do not accept a convenient explanation — NSAIDs, piles, 'poor diet' — as the cause of iron deficiency in an at-risk age group. This is the single commonest way a curable colorectal cancer is missed.
Never attribute rectal bleeding to haemorrhoids without visualising the colon.
A per-rectal examination is part of the examination, not an optional extra.
Do not transfuse chronic, well-compensated iron deficiency anaemia; treat with iron and treat the cause.
Check haemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected thalassaemia trait only after iron repletion, because iron deficiency suppresses HbA2.
